item.title: I Wrote 61 Tests for an AI Mentor. Then I Found Out Tests Can't Be Trusted Either
item.description:
You don't hire a tutor based on their resume. You give them a real student's notebook and see not whether they know the answer, but where they'll get stuck. Will they point out the line with the error, or rewrite the problem for the student? Will they say 'I don't know, let's check,' or confidently make something up? A month ago, I integrated an AI mentor into my educational platform: it sees lessons, student progress, and their latest attempt at a task. To avoid choosing a model and tweaking prompts based on gut feeling, I set up a testing environment with automated checks and started making decisions based on its metrics. A week later, I discovered the environment itself was flawed. It accepted incomplete answers, missed a complete solution submitted under a different variable name, and failed a correct refusal. Another week later, the model in the environment behaved flawlessly, but on production for the same class of questions – it didn't. This article is about how the testing environment is set up, what it helped solve, where it created false confidence, and how I ultimately stopped trusting the model altogether. Where the environment lied.

item.title: I Set Up a Project Institute for Small Models: Weak Sectioning Gave Fourfold Improvement, a Swarm Five Points
item.description:
I am a thermal engineer, head of a department in a design organization, with fourteen years in design. I've never been a programmer, and I've been tinkering with neural networks for less than a year. This spring, I set out to grow a swarm from weak local models that would be smarter than the strongest one. The swarm didn't get smarter. However, along the way, I broke down six small models according to the scheme that any design institute works by, and measured what this scheme can handle under load. Only sectioning holds up, and it benefits a weak model more than a strong one. Read more

item.title: Neural Network by Recipe: Calculating Weights Instead of Storing Matrices
item.description:
Neural network weights are a lot of digits in very large matrices. What if, instead of storing them, we stored a small recipe to calculate the necessary weights on the fly? Such approaches already exist, from a small network generating another network to formulas and actual fractals. Let's explore what works and what trade-offs are made for compactness. We'll also see how far LLMs are from the fate of the first Doom – being runnable on every teapot. Read on.

item.title: Odyssey-3: A World Model That Teaches Robots Physics from Video
item.description:
Imagine explaining to a child why a mug breaks when knocked off a table. You wouldn't start with the law of universal gravitation. A child sees hundreds of falling objects and naturally forms an understanding: things fall, hard objects break on impact, liquids spill. They absorb physics through observation, not textbooks. Now, imagine teaching a neural network the same way. Instead of showing it thousands of hours of the same task, let it watch a vast amount of video to understand the world. Then, equip it with arms, wheels, or propellers and teach it what to do with just tens of hours of data. This is Odyssey's bet. On September 15, 2026, they announced Odyssey-3, and on October 8, they released a research preview for everyone. This article will explore what this model is, how it was trained, where its record-breaking figures come from, and where facts end and marketing begins. Read more

item.title: How Google Taught a Tiny Model to Understand Text, Images, Video, and Audio: A Deep Dive into EmbeddingGemma 2
item.description:
On October 6, 2026, Google DeepMind released EmbeddingGemma 2, an open-source embedding model that converts text, code, images, video, and audio into vectors. All these vectors reside in a single, shared 768-dimensional space, enabling cross-modal comparisons, such as searching for videos using text queries. A key feature is its size: Google reports that on a Pixel 11 Pro, the text-only component uses about 191 MB of RAM, while the full multimodal version requires around 567 MB. This allows search functionalities to run directly on the device, eliminating the need to send data to a server. This article explores the model's architecture, its compact design, how to work with it, and potential pitfalls to be aware of.

item.title: [Translation] Eight Assumptions About Security That AI Agents Are Quietly Breaking
item.description:
Ben Lorica (Gradient Flow) analyzes recent AI agent attacks. In one hack, work estimated to take human operators two weeks took less than ten hours, and in the Hugging Face incident, about 17,600 agent actions were recovered over four and a half days. The exploits primarily used common weaknesses, but the attacker's persistence changed. This leads to eight practical takeaways: from the "detection to localization" metric and agent harness protection to temporary credentials and security boundaries beyond the model. Read more →
